system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 20 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2182-10-26 21:11:00 to 2182-11-15 16:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening dizziness and chronic abdominal pain, following a recent hospitalization for culture-negative peritonitis and orthostatic hypotension. She reported persistent dizziness even at rest, which worsened with standing, and generalized abdominal pain exacerbated by peritoneal dialysis. Initial peritoneal fluid showed elevated white blood cells, but repeat testing and cultures were negative for infection, and CT imaging revealed no abscess or acute abdominal process. Orthostatic blood pressure improved after increasing midodrine to 10 mg TID and fludrocortisone to 0.1 mg BID, and discontinuing tizanidine. Symptoms of dysuria resolved after fluconazole and restarting torsemide, with urine culture showing no significant growth. She was discharged on optimized medical therapy with follow-up arranged, and will continue peritoneal dialysis at home.
problems: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with diabetic autonomic (poly)neuropathy

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms ___,

WHY WERE YOU ADMITTED TO THE HOSPITAL? 
-You were admitted because you fractured your hip. 

WHAT HAPPENED WHILE YOU WERE HERE?
-You had surgery to repair the fracture in your hip and a nail 
was placed in the hip joint. 
-You pain was controlled with dilaudid. We also increased the 
dose of your nortriptyline and Lyrica to help the pain, and we 
restarted your tizanidine as well.  
-You were treated for a urinary tract infection. 
-Two new medications were started to help with your kidney 
disease: sodium bicarbonate and lanthanum. 
-Your nausea was controlled with anti-nausea medications. We 
also gave you an injection of a medicine called methylnaltrexone 
which helps with nausea and vomiting from opiate medicines like 
dilaudid and oxycodone. This improved your symptoms. This is not 
a ""long term"" medication, which is why it is important to wean 
off of the opiates as quickly and safely as you can!
-Physical therapy worked with you to improve the mobility in 
your leg. 
-Your peritoneal dialysis was continued. 
-You had a fall the day prior to discharge. Repeat x-rays were 
stable and you were monitored overnight.

WHAT SHOULD YOU DO WHEN YOU LEAVE THE HOSPITAL?
[ ] Continue physical therapy and occupational therapy. Use your 
rolling walker. 
[ ] Follow-up with your primary care doctor.
[ ] Follow up with your gastroenterologist  
[ ] Continue taking all of your medicines as prescribed. Do not 
mix the dilaudid and other prescriptions you may have at home, 
such as oxycodone.
[ ] Continue taking the new medicines (sodium bicarbonate and 
lanthanum) to treat your kidney disease. 
[ ] Talk to your endocrinologist about your insulin doses. You 
should take 4 units of glargine in the morning and 20 units in 
the evening until you are told to change it. Take your sliding 
scale insulin as instructed.

We wish you all the best in your recovery!

off of the opiates as quickly and safely as you can!

your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I know you just got transferred in. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I fell this morning while feeding my dog. I tried to grab the counter but slipped. My hip hurt so bad—I could tell something was wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the X-ray shows a left intertrochanteric hip fracture. We’ll need to fix that surgically. You’re stable for now, but we’ll get you prepped for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I’m nervous. I’ve had balance issues for years because of my neuropathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your diabetes and neuropathy do increase fall risk. But we’ll get the fracture fixed, and then focus on recovery and safety at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My sugars have been high too. I had 261 at the other hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your insulin. We’ll monitor closely. Your labs also show low sodium and potassium, which we’re correcting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis? I do peritoneal dialysis every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your daily peritoneal dialysis. The team will manage it while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for surgery today. Orthopedics will place a nail in your hip to stabilize the fracture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to walk again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most patients do well after this surgery. You’ll start physical therapy soon. But it will take time and rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery went well. You now have a cephalomedullary nail in your left hip. The alignment looks good on X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My hip still hurts, but I’m glad it’s fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Dilaudid for pain. But we’ll watch for side effects, especially nausea, since you have gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your peritoneal fluid was checked—no signs of infection. That’s good, given your history of peritonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling nauseous. I can’t keep much down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the pain meds might be making your gastroparesis worse. We tried Zofran, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take Reglan. It makes me so anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re giving you an injection called methylnaltrexone. It helps with opioid-related nausea without affecting pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed signs of infection, so we’re starting antibiotics for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having trouble urinating too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve had urinary retention. We placed a catheter, but now you’re doing intermittent straight cathing, which is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved since the methylnaltrexone. We’ll keep giving it for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel much better. I even ate a little toast this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re also adjusting your dialysis prescription to help with your acidosis and phosphorus levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started sodium bicarbonate for your metabolic acidosis. It’s common with kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new pill with meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s lanthanum. It helps control your phosphate levels. You couldn’t tolerate sevelamer before, so we’re trying this instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased your nortriptyline and Lyrica to help with your chronic nerve pain and fibromyalgia. They also help with depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so anxious. Is it okay to keep taking my clonazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve kept it, but at a lower dose. We’re also continuing your fluoxetine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy saw you yesterday. You’re starting to move your leg. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard, but I want to get back to walking with my cane.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need help at home. We’re arranging physical therapy 3 times a week and occupational therapy twice a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was high at first, but it’s coming down. That suggests your body is responding to the stress of the fracture and surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection in your peritoneal fluid or blood. Your UTI is being treated, and your symptoms are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting to reduce your IV pain meds and switch to oral Dilaudid. But we’ll taper it soon to avoid worsening nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about the pain coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep Tylenol on board and use the Dilaudid only as needed. The goal is to use the least amount possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin was low, so you got one unit of blood. It’s improved, which helps with healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, and kidney disease all contribute. We’re continuing your modafinil for energy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked another X-ray today. Your hip is healing well, no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been doing my exercises like PT said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Keep it up. We’re also restarting tizanidine for muscle spasms, 4mg twice a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has resolved. We’re stopping the methylnaltrexone. We’ll keep working on reducing the Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about being on it long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your insulin doses have been adjusted. You’ll go home with 4 units of glargine in the morning and 20 at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I change that later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Talk to your endocrinologist. They may adjust it based on your sugars. Keep using the sliding scale as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed the staples from your incision. It’s healing well. Steri-strips are in place now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It looks better. Still tender, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your UTI treatment is finishing up. You’ll complete the 10-day course before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another pelvic X-ray today—no changes. Your hip is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making good progress. We’re planning for discharge in a few days. You’ll go home with a rolling walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about being home alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged extra visiting nurse services because of your concerns. You won’t be alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall this morning, but the X-ray shows no new injury. We’ll watch you tonight and discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t see the rug. I’m so scared I’ll fall again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re sending PT and OT to your home. They’ll help make it safer and build your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. You’re doing well—hip stable, pain controlled, nausea gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds, especially the new ones—sodium bicarbonate and lanthanum. Use your walker. Do your exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it only as needed, no more than three times a day. We’re limiting it to avoid nausea. Call your doctor if pain isn’t controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—primary care, gastroenterologist, and endocrinologist. And keep all your home services. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready, but still a little scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. You’ve been through a lot. But you’re strong, and we’ve set you up for success. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and good luck with your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I take calcium or vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on calcitriol and Nephrocaps, which include what you need. But your doctor may consider a bisphosphonate later for osteoporosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep up with dialysis. The access site looks clean—no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned a lot this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Knowledge is power. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more confident already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. Now let’s get you home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up. Rest well and keep building your strength.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted following a mechanical fall that resulted in a left intertrochanteric femur fracture. She underwent successful open reduction and internal fixation with a cephalomedullary nail. Her hospital course was complicated by opioid-induced nausea and a gastroparesis flare, which resolved with methylnaltrexone. A urinary tract infection was treated with antibiotics, and urinary retention improved with intermittent catheterization. Her end-stage renal disease was managed with continued peritoneal dialysis, and metabolic acidosis was corrected with oral bicarbonate. Phosphate control was addressed with lanthanum due to intolerance of sevelamer. Chronic pain and fibromyalgia were managed with uptitrated nortriptyline and pregabalin, and tizanidine was restarted for muscle spasms. She participated in physical therapy, was transitioned to oral pain control, and was discharged home with home health services after an unwitnessed fall with stable repeat imaging.
